cues.text: Thank you all for coming here today to hear about the Moa, a kind of animal which has been extinct for a long time.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Well, first of all we’ll look at what the Moa are. The Moa are nine species of flightless birds endemic to  New Zealand.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: They were the dominant herbivores in New Zealand’s forest, shrubland and subalpine ecosystems for thousands of years, but around 500 years ago, they all went extinct.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: When I mention extinct animals during ancient times, you may immediately think of dinosaurs, which disappeared around 66 million years ago.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Fossils of dinosaurrs which we use to study are large in number, but not many of those of Moa remain, though both animals appeal to people today.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: So the Moa sound more mysterious now. But sir, I’ve got a question about these flightless birds.
cues.speaker: Student Female

cues.text: How can we distinguish them from other birds?
cues.speaker: Student Female

cues.text: That’s a good question! Birds are commonly characterised by being warm- blooded, having feathers and wings usually capable of flight, and laying eggs, while the flightless Moa.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: until their extinction, were the largest birds in the world. Their heads are relatively small in relation to their bodies, and they are the only wingless birds lacking even the vestigial wings and substantial tail bones in their family.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: That’s impressive. But were they bom to be like that? I mean when they were chicks.
cues.speaker: Student Male

cues.text: Yes, absolutely! So let’s move onto the chicks.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: The eggs of Moa were laid in nests and incubated for about two months.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: The chicks would be well- developed upon hatching and probably would be able to leave the nests to feed on their own almost immediately.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: I’ve heard that the male Moa are thought to have incubated the eggs. Is that true?
cues.speaker: Student Female

cues.text: I think there is a possibility for that.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: I’ve read somewhere that the sex- specific DNA recovered from the outer surfaces of eggshells suggested that these eggs were likely to have been hatched by the male, but we still need to consult more.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: But I have a question. There has been some occasional speculation that the Moa were still alive, because someone said they had caught sight of  them in New Zealand in the late 19th century or even the 20th.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Do you think it’s possible?
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: I’m not amazed by that, since that kind of thing has been claimed several times, but I find it funny because no reliable evidence of Moa tracks has ever been found, and experts still contend that Moa survival is extremely unlikely.
cues.speaker: Student Male

cues.text: So what was the reason for the Moa’s extinction? I wonder if it was global warming or some other factors related to their living environment.
cues.speaker: Student Female

cues.text: Well, before the arrival of human settlers in New Zealand, the Moa’s only predator was the massive Haas’s eagle.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Then  the Maori arrived sometime before CE 1300, and all Moa genera were soon driven to extinction by hunting. What a horrible thing
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: All right. Now let’s look at the features of some species of Moa.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: The South Island Giant Moa may have been the tallest birds ever known, and the second tallest of the nine moa species is the North Island Giant Moa, with the females being markedly larger than males both in weight and height.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: And I’ve heard that the smallest of the Moa birds are the Coastal Moa. Is that right?
cues.speaker: Student Male

cues.text: Yes, you’re right. And have you heard about any other kinds of Moa before?
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: I know the Crested Moa. The eggs they laid may be larger than others’.
cues.speaker: Student Female

cues.text: As they mainly lived in the remote interior of the Southern Island, their fossils are rare or absent in archaeological sites, and no egg remains have yet been identified.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Yes, of course.  A considerable amount of remains of the Stoutlegged Moa exist, due to the well-preserved properties of their habitat.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Yes, of course.  A considerable amount of remains of the Stoutlegged Moa exist, due to the well-preserved properties of their habitat.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Their skulls reveal relatively bad vision, a good sense of smell, and a very short bill.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: Then there is the Eastern Moa. They were remarkable in having very long and narrow windpipes, which probably enabled them to make louder, more resonant calls than those of other Moa, and have the greatest vocal abilities, so they could communicate when they could not see each other in the forest or at night.
cues.speaker: Lecturer

cues.text: They used a range of senses, apart from sound in their search for food, such as their sense of smell and vision.
cues.speaker: Lecturer
